articles.title: Young adults who fear rejection also tend to fear death more, psychology study finds
articles.summary: Young adults who worry about rejection tend to fear death more, a study of 640 Italians found. That fear was tied to more anxiety and related symptoms, but mainly among those who see death as final.

articles.title: How the menstrual cycle might alter ADHD symptoms in women taking stimulant medication
articles.summary: A new study reveals that ADHD symptoms peak in severity during menstruation for women taking stimulant medications. The findings suggest that natural hormonal fluctuations alter attention and mood, highlighting a need for highly personalized treatment plans.

articles.title: Dominance-seeking workers see more sexual interest in coworkers’ behavior, and that may help explain harassment
articles.summary: A smile or friendly chat at work isn’t usually an invitation. But employees with a strong desire to dominate others were more likely to read sexual interest into such behavior, and those perceptions were linked to self-reported harassment.

articles.summary: Children breathe a mix of pollution from cars, power plants, farms, and fires. A study of more than 6,000 U.S. kids found several sources were tied to their own pattern of brain network communication.

articles.summary: A new study finds that the practical disruptions of a romantic breakup, such as moving or changing finances, are associated with increased ambiguity around a person's sexual orientation.

articles.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
articles.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

articles.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
articles.summary: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

articles.title: Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side
articles.summary: A cannabis-derived ingredient commonly found in sleep gummies may be more habit-forming than previously thought, with new research showing that repeated exposure caused tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. Scientists warn that CBN may carry risks similar to THC, although its long-term effects in humans remain largely unknown.

articles.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.

articles.summary: Most research on the runner’s high has looked at workouts under an hour. New research on marathoners and ultramarathoners found the body’s cannabis-like chemicals remain active through hours of running.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: People with psychosis and a history of aggression are more likely to mistake negative emotions for positive ones
articles.summary: Misreading another person’s irritation or sadness as something positive could mean missing a cue to back off. A new study found this error was more common in people with psychotic disorders and a history of aggression.

articles.title: Expecting to lose economic standing hurts well-being more than expecting to gain helps it
articles.summary: Worrying about slipping down the socioeconomic ladder may take a psychological toll. Across four studies in Spain and the U.S., expecting downward mobility was tied to greater status anxiety, which in turn predicted lower life satisfaction.

articles.title: Breast reduction surgery is linked to improved sexual function
articles.summary: A new meta-analysis reveals that breast reduction surgery is linked to improvements in sexual desire, arousal, and satisfaction. Researchers suggest that alleviating physical pain and reducing appearance-related anxiety both play a role in enhancing postoperative sexual well-being.

articles.title: Emotional struggles are linked to vulnerable narcissism but not grandiose narcissism, meta-analysis finds
articles.summary: A meta-analysis of 26 studies involving more than 12,000 adults found that vulnerable narcissism was moderately linked to difficulty managing emotions, while grandiose narcissism showed virtually no connection.

articles.title: The psychology behind Taylor Swift’s billion-dollar media empire
articles.summary: The intense, one-sided connections fans feel toward Taylor Swift and their fear of missing out strongly predict whether they will attend her concerts and movies, highlighting how the psychological need for social belonging drives massive consumer behaviors.
